claims.claim: The council met at Clermont in Auvergne in November 1095
Urban II's letter for Grenoble is dated at Clermont on III Kalends of December (29 November), and speaks of the council which we held at Clermont, city of Auvergne
The act of concord between Cluny and La Chaise-Dieu was enacted publicly at Clermont and confirmed by Urban II, dated 1 December 1095, fourth indiction
Urban, seated in a raised pulpit, spoke of the sufferings of 'Christiani nostri fratres' in Jerusalem, Antioch and the other cities of the East
Some hearers wept, some trembled, some argued about it
Baldric says he watched ('nobis videntibus') as Adhémar, bishop of Le Puy ('Neimarus' in the OCR), came to the pope with a glad face, knelt, and asked and obtained leave and a blessing to go
Adhémar obtained an order from the pope that all should obey him, and he was to lead and protect the army
The nobles assented, and at once they all sewed the sign of the holy cross on their outer clothes
In Baldric's speech Urban tells those going to fit the cross to their clothes, to go more safely and be an example to others
Baldric was abbot of Bourgueil
Baldric was not on the crusade and reworked an anonymous history
The Histoire littéraire, reprinted by Migne, says Baldric was at the council of Clermont
Baldric's account is a history written up afterward with Urban's speech in his own Latin; William of Tyre gives a different speech
The council's acts are not among our sources; Mirbt prints canons 2 and 9, citing Mansi XX 816 and 902, a volume not held
Urban held a council at Piacenza and, fleeing the anger of the emperor (Henry IV), left Italy and crossed the Alps into the kingdom of the Franks
After the general council of Piacenza Urban came to Auvergne and held another general synod there with many bishops and abbots of Gaul
Powerful and honored men without number flowed to the council from many regions
William of Tyre: bishops and abbots from all the provinces beyond the Alps, with some princes present
Albert of Aachen: the bishops of all France, dukes, counts and great princes
William planned a general council first at Vézelay, then at Le Puy, before it met at Clermont
Albert: Urban decreed the council at Le Puy, then went on to Clermont
William of Tyre was writing in 1184
In William's telling Peter the Hermit brought Urban letters from the patriarch and faithful of Jerusalem
In William's telling the patriarch told Peter there was no hope from the Greeks, who had lost more than half their empire
In William's speech Urban says the letter was brought by Peter, 'qui praesens est'
William says canons of peace were made at Peter the Hermit's prompting, with canons for the reform of morals
Canon 2: whoever goes to free the church of God at Jerusalem 'pro sola devotione, non pro honoris vel pecmiiae adeptione' shall have the journey counted in place of all penance

Canon 9 (Codex Cencii): because many regions of Gaul were short of food, the truce to hold continuously for three years for peasants and merchants, for knights from Thursday to Sunday each week, for clerics and monks at all times, and first of all for pilgrims to the holy places

In William's speech Urban relaxes the penances of those who take arms for the pilgrimage, places their persons and goods under the church's protection, orders excommunication by the local bishop of anyone who harms them, and suspends bishops and priests who do not resist such men
By William's account the pope commanded those vowed to the journey to put the cross on their clothes and carry it on their shoulders
Adhémar was the first to receive the word, and William, bishop of Orange, followed
While this went on, envoys of Raymond, count of Toulouse, arrived without warning, said he would go and had already taken the cross, and bore witness to it in the council
Those faint-hearted the day before took courage
The council was dissolved and each hurried home; the bishops preached, lay people shouted it, and every day the number of those bound for Jerusalem grew
The bishops went home and worked, by the synod's statutes, to keep the truce unbroken
Princes who took the cross included Hugh the Great, Robert of Flanders, Robert of Normandy, Stephen of Blois, Adhémar, William of Orange, Raymond of Toulouse and Godfrey of Lorraine with his brothers
Robert of Flanders, hearing the decree of the council of Clermont, left wife and children and all he had
The Book of the Popes: Gregory VII had preached the journey to Jerusalem and could not do it because King Henry persecuted him
The Book of the Popes: the church would not let Urban go; with his blessing and absolution the crowds fought under him and blessed Peter
Anna Komnene is the daughter of the emperors Alexios and Irene
Anna: Alexios heard of countless Frankish armies coming and feared their unrestrained rush, their greed and their easy breaking of agreements
Anna traces the movement to Peter (Koukoupetros), who proclaimed in all the Latin lands that a divine voice bade him call the counts of Frankia to free Jerusalem

Anna: with the soldiers came an unarmed crowd more than the sand and the stars, with crosses on their shoulders, women and children who had left their lands, like rivers flowing together from everywhere
Ibn al-Athir: at Constantinople the emperor refused the Franks passage unless they swore to hand over Antioch, and they consented
Ibn al-Athir: the prince 'Bardouyl' offered Roger of Sicily help against Africa, Roger pointed him to Jerusalem; others say the caliphs of Egypt called the Franks
Matthew of Edessa: in the Armenian year 545 the peoples of Italy, Spain and the farthest nations of the Franks came to free Jerusalem, fulfilling the prophecy of Saint Nerses
Urban's letter: the Salmorenc quarrel was settled by the council's authority; clergy and laity there forbidden to obey the archbishop of Vienne until the judgment is carried out
Hugh of Grenoble laid his complaint against the archbishop before the pope and the whole assembly at the council in Auvergne
Hugh of Cluny and Pontius of La Chaise-Dieu made a concord at the council by the pope's hand, through Archbishops Hugh of Lyon and Aldebert of Bourges
Mansi's editors: the indulgence granted at Clermont to the defenders of the Eastern church was later granted for those going to Spain
Census edge latin-papal-church-gregorian to latin-church-of-outremer: Latin clergy filled the new sees in the East; the first Latin patriarch of Antioch had been chaplain to Adhémar (Dulaurier)
Peter, bishop of Pamplona, was at the council, by a Bollandist editor

contested_claims.sides: Peter the Hermit with the patriarch's letter: William of Tyre (WT l.5870-5874, 6318-6319) and Albert of Aachen (PL166 l.27786-27827). Gregory VII's earlier plan: the Book of the Popes (LP2 l.71356-71362). Peter alone, at a divine voice: Anna Komnene (ANNA l.15648-15666). A Frankish prince and Roger of Sicily, or the caliphs of Egypt: Ibn al-Athir (IBNA l.24668-24725). Prophecy of Saint Nerses: Matthew of Edessa (MATT l.12668-12678).

contested_claims.claim: Whether Peter the Hermit was at the council
contested_claims.sides: Yes: William of Tyre, later narrative (WT l.6122-6123, 6319). Not named: Baldric, present (PL166 l.77420-77760, searched; only 'beatus Petrus' of Antioch at 77494).
Baldric's version, written up by one who was present (PL166 l.77480-77695); William of Tyre's different version, written in 1184 (WT l.6130-6332). Neither is a transcript.

1095: William of Tyre (WT l.6066-6067), the act of concord (PL159 l.74964), Urban's letter with Le Couteulx's year (CART l.13240-13241, 13316), Mirbt (MIRBT l.11220), Duchesne (LP2 l.71663-71665). 1096: Migne's heading to the act (PL159 l.74878), the Bollandists (AASS-JUN5 l.148148-148149), and Baldric's printed 'anno subsequente (1096)' after a star-shower of April 1095 (PL166 l.77749-77751, 77773-77774), the bracket likely an editor's.

contested_claims.claim: Whether the council sat at Vézelay and Le Puy
contested_claims.sides: Planned or decreed only: William's Latin (WT l.6114-6115) and Albert (PL166 l.27895-27897). Sat there: the Old French Eracles (WT l.6140-6142), a translator's change.

contested_claims.claim: That Clermont prescribed the Hours of the Virgin for clergy
contested_claims.sides: Late writers cited by the editor of Bruno's Acta (Labbe, Petreius, Dorland, Blomevenna), who himself doubts parts (PL152 l.26632-26701). No ancient witness among our sources.

claims.claim: When the time came that the bishops began to go to Rome for the Lateran council, Dominic joined Fulk, bishop of Toulouse, so that they might go to the council together
From the death of the bishop of Osma to the Lateran council nearly ten years passed, in which Dominic stayed almost alone
Dominic and Fulk meant to ask Pope Innocent with one voice to confirm for Dominic and his companions an order to be called of Preachers
Jordan of Saxony, the author of the Libellus, was the second master general of the Order of Preachers
No account from inside the sessions is among our sources
claims.witness: dossier section 14 (searches for Wendover, Matthew Paris, Richard of San Germano, Ursberg, Vaux-de-Cernay, Tudela, Puylaurens over cic/texts)

claims.claim: The canons are held in extract in Mirbt's source book (nos. 277-282) and in Denzinger's Enchiridion (nos. 428-437)
Mirbt dates the council 11 to 30 November 1215
Hethum of Korykos counts 422 bishops and 72 archbishops at the council, under the Armenian year 664 (27 January 1215 to 26 January 1216 by the editors' conversion)
Hethum's chronological table was composed in 1296, by its title as the editors report it
The Maronites keep the customs and rites of the Latins as a sign of obedience, and so their patriarch was present at the general council of the Lateran under Innocent III
Pope Innocent held a general council to tear Jerusalem from the hands of the unbelievers

The notice in Mansi: Innocent called the Lateran synod, twelfth ecumenical, to correct the people's corrupt morals, condemn heretics and turn princes and people to recover the Holy Land, and presided over it
Canon 1: one true God alone, Father, Son and Holy Spirit
Canon 1: one universal church of the faithful, outside which no one at all is saved

Canon 1: Christ's body and blood are truly contained in the sacrament of the altar under the forms of bread and wine, the bread changed in substance into the body and the wine into the blood by God's power
Canon 1: only a rightly ordained priest can make this sacrament; baptism profits children and adults; the fallen can be restored by penance; married people too can reach eternal blessedness

Canon 21: every believer of either sex, past the age of discretion, is to confess all their sins at least once a year to their own priest, do the penance given and receive the Eucharist at least at Easter, unless their own priest advises abstaining for a time for a reasonable cause; otherwise barred from the church in life and denied Christian burial
Canon 21: a priest who reveals a sin heard in confession is deposed and shut in a strict monastery for perpetual penance

Canon 3: secular powers are to swear publicly to drive out from their lands all heretics marked out by the church; a lord who will not cleanse his land is excommunicated, and after a year the pope may free his vassals and offer the land to Catholics

Canon 3: every heresy against the catholic faith is excommunicated, all heretics condemned by whatever names they go; the condemned are left to the secular powers; suspects who do not clear themselves are excommunicated and after a year condemned
Canon 3: Catholics who take the cross against heretics receive the indulgence granted for the Holy Land
Canon 3: those who, prohibited or not sent, preach without authority from the apostolic see or the catholic bishop of the place are excommunicated
Canon 3: bishops are to visit any parish where heretics are said to live once or twice a year and put men on oath to name heretics; a negligent bishop is to be deposed
Canon 3 names no group; Albigenses and Waldenses are Denzinger's headings

Canon 4: since the Greek church withdrew from obedience to the apostolic see, Greeks would not offer the sacrifice on altars where Latin priests had celebrated until they had washed them, as though defiled, and rebaptized those the Latins baptized; some, as the council has heard, still do

Canon 4: the council wishes to cherish and honor the Greeks returning to obedience, bearing with their customs as far as it can in the Lord; it forbids these practices that there may be one fold and one shepherd, on pain of excommunication and deposition
Canon 5: after Rome, Constantinople holds first place, Alexandria second, Antioch third, Jerusalem fourth

The Pedalion calls the council the local synod held in the Lateran of Rome in 1215 and cites its fourth canon on the Easterners not celebrating where a Westerner had celebrated without first a blessing of water, and on their rebaptizing, by the testimony of their own enemies
The Pedalion's commentary is by Agapios the hieromonk and Nikodemos the Hagiorite, first printed at Leipzig in 1800

Canon 2 condemns the tract Abbot Joachim put out against Peter Lombard on the unity or essence of the Trinity, calling him a heretic and a madman for saying in his Sentences that there is one supreme reality which is Father, Son and Holy Spirit

Canon 2 reports that Joachim held Lombard taught a quaternity, the three persons and the common essence as a fourth, and that the unity of the three was collective and by likeness, as many people are called one people
With the council's approval the pope believed and confessed with Peter Lombard; whoever defends Joachim's teaching on this point is to be refuted as a heretic

In his Tractatus, Joachim warns against thinking of the three as three branches fixed in one root, the substance as root and the hypostases as branches, which is to bring in a quaternity; Buonaiuti's bracket says the allusion is to Peter Lombard

Canon 2 spares the monastery of Fiore, because its rule is sound and its observance wholesome, and above all because Joachim ordered all his writings handed to the apostolic see for approval or correction, in a letter he signed with his own hand
Joachim's letter of submission, signed with his own hand in 1200, asks that his works be presented to the apostolic see for correction
claims.witness: acta-sanctorum_maii-tomus-6-lat_1739.txt l.80610-80612, 80638-80660, 80676-80679 (right column of interleaved OCR)

claims.claim: Canon 2 condemns the teaching of Almaric as not so much heretical as mad, without stating it
Innocent told Dominic to go back to his brothers, choose with them a rule already approved and return for confirmation; with the council over, they went back and chose the rule of Augustine
Pope Honorius confirmed the Order
The Bollandists connect Innocent's answer with canon 13, which they quote from Labbe
Canon 13, as quoted: so that too great a variety of religious orders does not bring confusion, no one is to found a new order; whoever wishes to enter religion is to take one already approved

Jacques de Vitry came to Perugia and found Pope Innocent dead but not yet buried; in the night his precious robes had been stolen and his body left almost naked and stinking in the church; Vitry saw how short and empty is the deceiving glory of this world
The cardinals elected Honorius the next day
Vitry's letter I is dated October 1216 by Röhricht's heading
Innocent died at Perugia in 1216 (July: XVI Kal. Aug. by the notice in Mansi after the Ursberg chronicler and by Glassberger; X Kal. Aug. by the Assisi catalogue)

Honorius III to the bishop of Lucca, 2 December 1216 (fourth Nones of December, first year): forbids him to defame the abbot and monks of Fiore as heretics on the ground that Innocent condemned Joachim's tract with the general council's approval
claims.witness: acta-sanctorum_maii-tomus-6-lat_1739.txt l.80602-80634 (left column of interleaved OCR)

claims.claim: A letter of Honorius dated sixth Kalends of January in his fifth year (27 December 1220) orders it proclaimed through all Calabria that he holds Joachim to have been a Catholic man
claims.witness: acta-sanctorum_maii-tomus-6-lat_1739.txt l.80581-80601 (right column), with the address at l.80639

claims.claim: Lea: in 1220 the monks of Fiore procured from Honorius III a bull declaring Joachim a good Catholic
Denifle: the Lateran censure of Joachim's Trinitarian teaching stands in the Decretals of Gregory IX (1, 1)
The Anagni commission of 1255 judged that a passage of the Concordia seemed still to assert the heresy condemned in the Lateran council
Salimbene: the pope ordained there should be henceforth no new order of religious mendicants, but this was not kept through the negligence of the prelates
Lea: at the Council of Lyon in 1274 the Lateran canon prohibiting unauthorized orders was renewed, and the Carmelites and Augustinians were allowed to exist on sufferance
Trent's eighth canon on penance anathematizes anyone who says the faithful are not bound to confess once a year according to the constitution of the great Lateran council
Vitry, end of March 1217: the Maronite patriarch with his archbishops, bishops and people left all errors and submitted to the Catholic faith and the obedience of the Roman church
Letters went out from the pope in 1213 about calling a council, beginning Vineam Domini Sabaoth
claims.witness: laurentius-de-brezova_historia-hussitica-lat-ces_goll1893.txt l.14999-15000 (manuscript variant in the editor's note)

claims.claim: The council was held in the Lateran basilica in Innocent's eighteenth year, and almost the body of the whole universal church came together
Al-Duwayhi gives 411 bishops from the East and the West, names the patriarch Jeremiah and says the pope confirmed him and gave him the pallium (paraphrase; second witness only)
Dionysius O'Lonargan, archbishop of Cashel, died at Rome; Conar O'Heney, bishop of Killaloe, died on his return from the fourth General Council of Lateran (under 1215)

The Annals of Ulster, A.D. 1216: Eghdon Mac Gilluir, coarb of Patrick and primate of Ireland, died at Rome after the general Lateran council; the Annals of Kilronan, 1216: a synod of the clergy of the world at Rome at Lateran with Pope Innocent
Glassberger: Francis met Dominic at the council, to which Dominic had come with Fulk for approval of his order

Crusade decree: by the common approval of the council, all clergy give a twentieth of church income for three years to the Holy Land, some religious and the crusaders excepted; the pope and cardinals pay a full tenth
Canons 23-26 on episcopal elections; canon 62: old relics not shown outside their case or sold, new ones not publicly venerated without the Roman pontiff's approval
Canon 5 calls the Roman church mother and teacher of all Christ's faithful

contested_claims.sides: 422 bishops and 72 archbishops: Hethum of Korykos (rhc-armeniens_documents-armeniens-t1-fra_academie1869.txt l.54609-54612). 411 bishops from the East and the West: al-Duwayhi, second witness only (duwayhi_tarikh-al-ta-ifa-al-maruniyya-ara_shartuni1890.txt l.9488-9489). An unreadable OCR figure: the notice in Mansi (innocent-iii_opera-with-gesta-innocentii-pl214-lat_migne1853.txt l.1038). 'Almost the body of the whole universal church', no number: the Assisi catalogue (ehrle-denifle_archiv-literatur-kirchengeschichte-mittelalters-bd1-deu-lat_1885.txt l.26432-26433). 'More than four hundred bishops and eight hundred abbots': the census, from references not held.

11 to 30 November 1215: Mirbt (mirbt_quellen-zur-geschichte-des-papsttums-3e-aufl-deu-lat_1911.txt l.12278). 11 November 1215: Alishan, who misnames it a council at Lyon (alishan_leon-le-magnifique-et-table-chronologique-de-sissouan-fra_alishan1888.txt l.12467-12469). No source among ours from the time gives a month or day.

1215: the Four Masters (four-masters_annals-of-the-kingdom-of-ireland-v3-1172-1378-gle-eng_odonovan1856.txt l.16099-16108), Glassberger (glassberger_chronica-analecta-franciscana-v2-lat_1887.txt l.2110), Hethum's year 664 (rhc-armeniens_documents-armeniens-t1-fra_academie1869.txt l.54605). 1216: the Annals of Ulster and of Kilronan as O'Donovan quotes them (four-masters_annals-of-the-kingdom-of-ireland-v3-1172-1378-gle-eng_odonovan1856.txt l.16505-16513, 16632-16637), an annal-year difference.

contested_claims.claim: Whether the council was general (ecumenical) or local
contested_claims.sides: Twelfth ecumenical: Denzinger's heading (denzinger_enchiridion-symbolorum-lat_bannwart1911.txt l.13857) and the notice in Mansi (innocent-iii_opera-with-gesta-innocentii-pl214-lat_migne1853.txt l.1036-1037); general council: Vitry (jacques-de-vitry_historia-orientalis-et-occidentalis-lat_1597.txt l.10743-10744), the Assisi catalogue (ehrle-denifle_archiv-literatur-kirchengeschichte-mittelalters-bd1-deu-lat_1885.txt l.26432), the Four Masters (four-masters_annals-of-the-kingdom-of-ireland-v3-1172-1378-gle-eng_odonovan1856.txt l.16108). Local synod: the Pedalion (nikodemos-hagiorite_pedalion-canons-grc_1886.txt l.7141-7142). A pretended general council: Covel, Anglican, 1722 (covel_some-account-of-the-present-greek-church_1722.txt l.4909).

contested_claims.claim: Whether Francis of Assisi was at the council
contested_claims.sides: Yes: Glassberger alone (glassberger_chronica-analecta-franciscana-v2-lat_1887.txt l.2110-2112). Against: no early Franciscan source among ours names the council (dossier section 14 searches of Thomas of Celano, Bonaventure, Francis, Speculum perfectionis).

Any new religious order: the Bollandists' quotation from Labbe (acta-sanctorum_augusti-tomus-1-lat_1750.txt l.74820-74827). A new order of religious mendicants: Salimbene, with Coulton's bracket [new] (salimbene_from-st-francis-to-dante_coulton1907.txt l.13490-13492).

XVI Kal. Aug. (17 July) 1216: the notice in Mansi after the Ursberg chronicler (innocent-iii_opera-with-gesta-innocentii-pl214-lat_migne1853.txt l.1066-1070) and Glassberger (glassberger_chronica-analecta-franciscana-v2-lat_1887.txt l.2118). X Kal. Aug. (23 July): the Assisi catalogue (ehrle-denifle_archiv-literatur-kirchengeschichte-mittelalters-bd1-deu-lat_1885.txt l.26437-26438). Vitry saw him dead and unburied at Perugia (jacques-de-vitry_briefe-in-zeitschrift-fuer-kirchengeschichte-14-lat-deu_rohricht1894.txt l.5934-5940).

contested_claims.claim: Whether the Calabria passage and the date 27 December 1220 belong to Honorius's letter to Cosenza and Bisignano
contested_claims.sides: Read as one letter: the right column at acta-sanctorum_maii-tomus-6-lat_1739.txt l.80581-80601 continues the left column's address at l.80639, in an interleaved two-column OCR; the page image is unchecked. Lea agrees on a bull of 1220 declaring Joachim a good Catholic (lea_history-of-the-inquisition-of-the-middle-ages-v3_1888.txt l.1008-1013).

claims.claim: Before the council at Lyon had ended, Jerome of Ascoli came back with solemn envoys of the Greeks; cardinals, archbishops, bishops and a very great crowd of prelates went out half a league to meet them, and the pope received them with a kiss and tears of joy

While Gregory X celebrated solemn Mass, the Greeks sang the Creed with the article on the procession of the Holy Spirit three times over, taught by their interpreter John of Balastri, a Friar Minor of Constantinople learned in Greek and Latin
Glassberger was writing his chronicle in 1508
Gregory X began to hold at Lyon the general council he had called, on the feast of the apostles Philip and James; the editors' note gives 1 May
At the opening Gregory told a dream in which Christ promised that the church through him would win back the Holy Land and the Greeks
Gregory had sent Jerome of Ascoli and companions to bring the Greeks and the Tatars back to the unity of the church
Manuel Kalekas says the Roman pontiff was present in person, as the one who called it, with about four hundred bishops, and envoys of the church of Constantinople standing in its place
Fabricius says Kalekas, a Greek who wrote for the Latins, did not live at the time of the council of Lyon; a codex note says he died at Mytilene in 1410
Thomas Aquinas was going to the general council at Lyon by order of Gregory X, carrying the little book he had written at Pope Urban's order against the Greeks, and fell ill at the castle of Maenza
Thomas was summoned to the council and set out in Lent, a witness at his canonization said, though he did not remember the month or day
Nicholas, abbot of Fossanova, deposed that Thomas, summoned to the council of Lyon, fell ill at Maenza and was carried to Fossanova, where he lay ill about a month; he was buried at Fossanova
The council confessed that the Holy Spirit proceeds eternally from the Father and the Son, not as from two principles but as from one, not by two spirations but by one
With the approval of the council, Gregory condemned those who deny that the Spirit proceeds eternally from the Father and the Son, or say he proceeds as from two principles
The profession of faith of Michael VIII says the holy Roman Church holds supreme and full primacy over the whole Catholic Church, and that questions of faith must be settled by its judgment
Bannwart, Denzinger's editor, notes that the profession was put to Michael Palaiologos by Clement IV in 1267 and offered by him to Gregory X at the Second Council of Lyon
Ubi periculum: the cardinals wait ten days for the absent, then all live together in one conclave in the palace, closed on every side so that no one can go in or out
If no pope is chosen within three days of entering the conclave, the cardinals have one dish at lunch and supper for the next five days; after that only bread, wine and water, until a pope is chosen
Bonaventure fell ill while the council was still sitting, received full absolution from the pope's hand and died, to the dismay of the whole council
Greeks and Latins, religious, clergy and lay people followed Bonaventure's body with bitter tears to burial in the Franciscans' church at Lyon
Eubel's note dates Bonaventure's death to 15 July 1274, while he presided at the council
Gennadios Scholarios says Michael, warding off the Latins' revenge for the city, wished to make his rule safe for himself and his sons
Gennadios says the emperor deceived the church, saying he would make the union as an oikonomia, but chose envoys who knew his mind, and they came back bringing open Latinism
After Michael's death, Gennadios says, the act at Lyon was overturned by a great and splendid synod
The chronicle printed under Sphrantzes's name says the union rested on three heads: the pope named in the hymns, appeal to him, and his first place in all things

The same chronicle says the clergy would not keep quiet and stirred up the crowd, and that the emperor called it oikonomia, not innovation, and flogged, maimed and exiled many who would not be persuaded
The same chronicle says Michael, fearing Baldwin and Charles, sent envoys about union if only to block their expedition; it names Pope Alexander

The Directorium, in Miélot's French, says Michael, fearing Charles of Sicily would take his empire, turned to tricks, sending messengers to the council at Lyon while paying Peter of Aragon to seize Sicily
The Synaxaristes says Joseph would not accept the union Michael negotiated with Gregory X and gave up his throne, and the Latin-minded John Bekkos became patriarch

The patriarch list in PG 147 says Joseph, abbot of Galesion, was driven out by Michael because of the union with the Latins, and that Bekkos made the union under Michael and was cast down and exiled by Andronikos
The Synaxaristes remembers the twenty-six monks of Zographou, Euthymios abbot of Vatopedi and twelve Vatopedi monks as martyrs who rebuked the Latin-minded Michael and Bekkos
The Recueil editors say Michael signed the act of union in 1277 and Martin IV excommunicated him on 18 November 1281
Boulliau's note says Andronikos deprived his dead father of funeral pomp and the usual honors because he had sided with the Latins
Glassberger says three Franciscan prelates, Bonaventure, Eudes Rigaud of Rouen and the bishop of Tripoli, presided by the pope's order and handled the council's business
Envoys of the Tatars came in robes woven with gold to make an alliance, and a king's son among them was baptized, the pope lifting him from the font
Glassberger says the pope decreed with the council that there should be only two mendicant orders, the others dissolved until further order

Clement XIV says Gregory X at Lyon renewed Innocent III's constitution against new orders and banned for ever the mendicant orders founded after the Fourth Lateran Council without the apostolic see's confirmation
Boniface VIII later set the Augustinian Hermits and the Carmelites on a firm footing, as they had been before the council
Lea says the Carmelites and Augustinians were allowed to exist on sufferance until further order, and that Gregory vainly tried at Lyon to unite the military orders
The pope charged the bishops, and above all the Franciscans and Dominicans, to preach the cross in aid of the Holy Land
A council at Ravenna in 1311 ordered for vacant cathedrals what the Gregorian constitution Ubi periculum set for the Roman see
Clement V in 1309 gave the Oxford Franciscans the house of the Friars of the Penitence of Jesus Christ, left at the apostolic see's disposal under Gregory X's constitution at Lyon
Glassberger says the Greeks recognized the primacy of the Roman church and afterwards fell back into their old errors
In 1870 the First Vatican Council said that, with the approval of the Second Council of Lyon, the Greeks professed that the holy Roman Church enjoys supreme and full primacy
The same passage of Pastor aeternus in Latin

contested_claims.claim: How Patriarch Joseph I lost his throne
contested_claims.sides: Gave it up because he would not accept the union: the Synaxaristes, citing Meletios (nikodemos-hagiorite_synaxaristes-vol1-sep-feb-grc_1900.txt l.24169-24173). Driven out by the emperor Michael because of the union: the patriarch list in PG 147 (nicephorus-callistus_historia-ecclesiastica-with-hesychast-tracts-pg147-grc-lat_migne1865.txt l.21368-21371; Migne's Latin at l.21296-21297 mistranslates it). Ducange, citing Pachymeres (not held), dates his withdrawal to 11 January 1274 (gregoras_byzantina-historia-v2-grc-lat_schopen1830.txt l.38329-38333).

The feast of Philip and James, 1 May by the Quaracchi editors: Glassberger (glassberger_chronica-analecta-franciscana-v2-lat_1887.txt l.7157-7158, 7205). 7 May: Creyghton, 1660 (syropoulos_vera-historia-unionis-non-verae-grc-lat_creyghton1660.txt l.3059).

contested_claims.claim: Who the Greek envoys were, and whether a patriarch came
contested_claims.sides: Theophanes of Nicaea and the former patriarch Germanos: Creyghton (syropoulos_vera-historia-unionis-non-verae-grc-lat_creyghton1660.txt l.3061-3063). The emperor's patriarch: Guillaume Adam, hostile, about 1317 (rhc-armeniens_documents-armeniens-t2-latins-et-francais-fra_academie1906.txt l.63721-63722), whom the Recueil editors' introduction and index identify as Bekkos (l.17950-17952, 94775-94780); their own note makes Bekkos a resister in 1274 who replaced Joseph (l.63805-63812). Unnamed: Glassberger (glassberger_chronica-analecta-franciscana-v2-lat_1887.txt l.7246), Gennadios (gennadius-scholarius_opera-omnia-pg160-grc-lat_migne1866.txt l.67360).

Glassberger (glassberger_chronica-analecta-franciscana-v2-lat_1887.txt l.7173-7177) and Eubel (bullarium-franciscanum_v5-lat_eubel1898.txt l.91104-91107), both Franciscan. No held witness from outside the order confirms or denies it.

To ward off a Western attack or the Latins' revenge: Gennadios (gennadius-scholarius_opera-omnia-pg160-grc-lat_migne1866.txt l.67371-67376), the chronicle under Sphrantzes's name (sphrantzes-cananus-anagnostes_chronicles-grc-lat_bekker1838.txt l.1205-1213), the Directorium in Miélot's French (rhc-armeniens_documents-armeniens-t2-latins-et-francais-fra_academie1906.txt l.54214-54225). The census tradition entry byzantine-church-after-1054 says he needed help from the West; no held witness says so.

Remembered as martyrs who rebuked Michael and Bekkos: the Synaxaristes (nikodemos-hagiorite_synaxaristes-vol1-sep-feb-grc_1900.txt l.10268-10271, 47818-47828). Philipp Meyer, 1894: the story of a punitive invasion is hard to square with Michael's methods and may be confused with a Catalan raid after 1300 (athos-monasteries_haupturkunden-fur-die-geschichte-der-athoskloster-ger-grc_meyer1894.txt l.2931-2939).

Without funeral pomp and the usual honors: Boulliau (doukas_historia-byzantina-grc-lat_bekker1834.txt l.32497-32501). Left unburied: Creyghton (syropoulos_vera-historia-unionis-non-verae-grc-lat_creyghton1660.txt l.3090-3094); Guillaume Adam, hostile, says the monks made Andronikos swear never to let him be buried (rhc-armeniens_documents-armeniens-t2-latins-et-francais-fra_academie1906.txt l.63744-63748).

contested_claims.claim: What Lyon decided, in later Greek memory
contested_claims.sides: A union on Latin terms: Gennadios (gennadius-scholarius_opera-omnia-pg160-grc-lat_migne1866.txt l.67359-67368), Doukas (doukas_historia-byzantina-grc-lat_bekker1834.txt l.14310-14312), Kalekas (calecas_opera-omnia-pg152-grc-lat_migne1866.txt l.15006-15010). That it condemned the Latins and the acts were corrupted: an anti-unionist as portrayed by the unionist Joseph of Methone (chalcocondyles_historiarum-libri-x-with-isidore-leonard-plusiadenos-pg159-grc-lat_migne1866.txt l.56894-56912).

contested_claims.claim: Whether Manuel Kalekas was at Lyon
contested_claims.sides: Creyghton and Galesinius put him there (per the dossier, syropoulos_vera-historia-unionis-non-verae-grc-lat_creyghton1660.txt l.2288-2289; calecas_opera-omnia-pg152-grc-lat_migne1866.txt l.17894-17895, not rechecked). Fabricius says he lived later (calecas_opera-omnia-pg152-grc-lat_migne1866.txt l.365-371), and a codex note gives his death in 1410 (l.388).

absent_details.detail: The full acts (Mansi tomus 24)
absent_details.note: Not held; only the constitution on the Spirit, Michael's profession and Ubi periculum, in Denzinger's and Mirbt's extracts.

absent_details.detail: A list of those present
absent_details.note: Not held; Kalekas says the acts recorded names and ranks, but those records are not among our sources.

absent_details.detail: The closing day and the number of sessions
absent_details.note: No held source gives them.

absent_details.detail: A Greek account from the time, for or against the union
absent_details.note: None among our sources; Pachymeres, Akropolites and Gregoras's first volume are not held, and the Greek witnesses held date from the 1400s on.

absent_details.detail: Joseph I's own words
absent_details.note: Not held.

absent_details.detail: The text of the decree on the mendicant orders (Religionum diversitatem), the crusade decree Zelus fidei and the usury decree
absent_details.note: Not held; the mendicant decree is known through Glassberger, Clement XIV and Lea, and the usury decree only through later statutes citing it.

absent_details.detail: Names of the Tatar envoys and of the baptized prince
absent_details.note: Not held.

absent_details.detail: That the Creed was sung in Greek and Latin
absent_details.note: No held line says so; Glassberger says only that the interpreter knew both languages.

absent_details.detail: Gregory X's letter of summons
absent_details.note: Not held.
